entries.a6aada61fb3808b7b6c356a9e9661b7c58850bd5: <div sID="gen15904" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Isa.21" sID="Isa.21"/> <div eID="gen15904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15905" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15906" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have a prophecy of sad times coming, and heavy burdens, I. Upon Babylon, here called "the desert of the sea," that it should be destroyed by the Medes and Persians with a terrible destruction, which yet God's people should have advantage by, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.1-Isa.21.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. Upon Dumah, or Idumea, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11-Isa.21.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. III. Upon Arabia, or Kedar, the desolation of which country was very near, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.13-Isa.21.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. These and other nations which the princes and people of Israel had so much to do with the prophets of Israel could not but have something to say to. Foreign affairs must be taken notice of as well as domestic ones, and news from abroad enquired after as well as news at home.
entries.d285ab0522516f0baac2e0a9444e863f1dd6fba8: <div eID="gen15906" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15905" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 714.)</title> <div sID="gen15907" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds in the south pass through; <hi type="italic">so</hi> it cometh from the desert, from a terrible land. <hi type="super">2</hi> A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing <hi type="italic">of it;</hi> I was dismayed at the seeing <hi type="italic">of it.</hi> <hi type="super">4</hi> My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me. <hi type="super">5</hi> Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, <hi type="italic">and</hi> anoint the shield. <hi type="super">6</hi> For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he saw a chariot <hi type="italic">with</hi> a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a chariot of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed: <hi type="super">8</hi> And he cried, A lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime, and I am set in my ward whole nights: <hi type="super">9</hi> And, behold, here cometh a chariot of men, <hi type="italic">with</hi> a couple of horsemen. And he answered and said, Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground. <hi type="super">10</hi> O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you. <div eID="gen15907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15908" type="x-p"/> We had one burden of Babylon before (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.1-Isa.13.22">ch. xiii.</reference>); here we have another prediction of its fall. God saw fit thus to possess his people with the belief of this event by line upon line, because Babylon sometimes pretended to be a friend to them (as <reference osisRef="Isa.39.1">ch. xxxix. 1</reference>), and God would hereby warn them not to trust to that friendship, and sometimes was really an enemy to them, and God would hereby warn them not to be afraid of that enmity. Babylon is marked for ruin; and all that believe God's prophets can, through that glass, see it tottering, see it tumbling, even when with an eye of sense they see it flourishing and sitting as a queen. Babylon is here called the <hi type="italic">desert</hi> or <hi type="italic">plain of the sea;</hi> for it was a flat country, and full of lakes, or loughs (as they call them in Ireland), like little seas, and was abundantly watered with the many streams of the river Euphrates. Babylon did but lately begin to be famous, Nineveh having outshone it while the monarchy was in the Assyrian hands; but in a little time it became the lady of kingdoms; and, before it arrived at that pitch of eminency which it was at in Nebuchadnezzar's time, God by this prophet plainly foretold its fall, again and again, that his people might not be terrified at its rise, nor despair of relief in due time when they were its prisoners, <reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job v. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35-Ps.37.36">Ps. xxxvii. 35, 36</reference>. Some think it is here called a <hi type="italic">desert</hi> because, though it was now a populous city, it should in time be made a desert. And <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the destruction of Babylon is so often prophesied of by this evangelical prophet, because it was typical of the destruction of the man of sin, the great enemy of the New-Testament church, which is foretold in the <hi type="italic">Revelation</hi> in many expressions borrowed from these prophecies, which therefore must be consulted and collated by those who would understand the prophecy of that book. Here is, <div eID="gen15908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15909" type="x-p"/> I. The powerful irruption and descent which the Medes and Persians should make upon Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1-Isa.21.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): They will come <hi type="italic">from the desert, from a terrible land.</hi> The northern parts of Media and Persia, where their soldiers were mostly bred, was waste and mountainous, terrible to strangers that were to pass through it and producing soldiers that were very formidable. <hi type="italic">Elam</hi> (that is, Persia) is summoned to go up against Babylon, and, in conjunction with the forces of Media, to besiege it. When God has work of this kind to do he will find, though it be in a desert, in a terrible land, proper instruments to be employed in it. These forces come <hi type="italic">as whirlwinds from the south,</hi> so suddenly, so strongly, so terribly, such a mighty noise shall they make, and throw down every thing that stands in their way. As is usual in such a case, some deserters will go over to them: <hi type="italic">The treacherous dealers will deal treacherously.</hi> Historians tell us of Gadatas and Gobryas, two great officers of the king of Babylon, that went over to Cyrus, and, being well acquainted with all the avenues of the city, led a party directly to the palace, where Belshazzar was slain. Thus with the help of the <hi type="italic">treacherous dealers the spoilers spoiled.</hi> Some read it thus: <hi type="italic">There shall be a deceiver of that deceiver, Babylon, and a spoiler of that spoiler,</hi> or, which comes all to one, <hi type="italic">The treacherous dealer has found one that deals treacherously, and the spoiler one that spoils,</hi> as it is expounded, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">ch. xxxiii. 1</reference>. The Persians shall pay the Babylonians in their own coin; those that by fraud and violence, cheating and plundering, unrighteous wars and deceitful treaties, have made a prey of their neighbours, shall meet with their match, and by the same methods shall themselves be made a prey of. <div eID="gen15909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15910" type="x-p"/> II. The different impressions made hereby upon those concerned in Babylon. 1. To the poor oppressed captives it would be welcome news; for they had been told long ago that Babylon's destroyer would be their deliverer, and therefore, "when they hear that Elam and Media are coming up to besiege Babylon, <hi type="italic">all their sighing will be made to cease;</hi> they shall no longer mingle their tears with Euphrates' streams, but resume their harps, and smile when they remember Zion, which, before, they wept at the thought of." For the sighing of the needy the God of pity will arise in due time (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Ps. xii. 5</reference>); he will break the yoke from all their neck, will remove the rod of the wicked from off their lot, and so make their sighing to cease. 2. To the proud oppressors it would be a grievous vision (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">v. 2</reference>), particularly to the king of Babylon for the time being, and it should seem that he it is who is here brought in sadly lamenting his inevitable fate (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.3-Isa.21.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore are my loins filled with pain; pangs have taken hold upon me, &c.,</hi> which was literally fulfilled in Belshazzar, for that very night in which his city was taken, and himself slain, upon the sight of a hand writing mystic characters upon the wall <hi type="italic">his countenance was changed and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed and his knees smote one against another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.5.6">Dan. v. 6</reference>. And yet that was but the beginning of sorrows. Daniel's deciphering the writing could not but increase his terror, and the alarm which immediately followed of the executioners at the door would be the completing of it. And those words, <hi type="italic">The night of my pleasure has he turned into fear to me,</hi> plainly refer to that aggravating circumstance of Belshazzar's fall that he was slain on that night when he was in the height of his mirth and jollity, with his cups and concubines about him and a thousand of his lords revelling with him; that night of his pleasure, when he promised himself an undisturbed unallayed enjoyment of the most exquisite gratifications of sense, with a particular defiance of God and religion in the profanation of the temple vessels, was the night that was turned into all this fear. Let this give an effectual check to vain mirth and sensual pleasures, and forbid us ever to lay the reins on the neck of them—that we know not what heaviness the mirth may end in, nor how soon laughter may be turned into mourning; but this we know that for all these things God shall bring us into judgment; let us therefore mix trembling always with our joys. <div eID="gen15910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15911" type="x-p"/> III. A representation of the posture in which Babylon should be found when the enemy should surprise it—all in festival gaiety (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.5">v. 5</reference>): "Prepare the table with all manner of dainties. Set the guards; let them watch in the watch-tower while we eat and drink securely and make merry; and, if any alarm should be given, the princes shall arise and anoint the shield, and be in readiness to give the enemy a warm reception." Thus secure are they, and thus do they gird on the harness with as much joy as if they were putting it off. <div eID="gen15911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15912" type="x-p"/> IV. A description of the alarm which should be given to Babylon upon its being forced by Cyrus and Darius. The Lord, in vision, showed the prophet the watchman set in his watch-tower, near the watch-tower, near the palace, as is usual in times of danger; the king ordered those about him to post a sentinel in the most advantageous place for discovery, and, according to the duty of a watchman, let <hi type="italic">him declare what he sees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.6">v. 6</reference>. We read of watchmen thus set to receive intelligence in the story of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.24">2 Sam. xviii. 24</reference>), and in the story of Jehu, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.17">2 Kings ix. 17</reference>. This watchman here discovered a chariot with a couple of horsemen attending it, in which we may suppose the commander-in-chief to ride. He then saw another chariot drawn by asses or mules, which were much in use among the Persians, and a chariot drawn by camels, which were likewise much in use among the Medes; so that (as Grotius thinks) these two chariots signify the two nations combined against Babylon, or rather these chariots come to bring tidings to the palace; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.31-Jer.51.32">Jer. li. 31, 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to show the king of Babylon that his city is taken at one end</hi> while he is revelling at the other end and knows nothing of the matter. The watchman, seeing these chariots at some distance, <hi type="italic">hearkened diligently with much heed,</hi> to receive the first tidings. And (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.8">v. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">he cried, A lion;</hi> this word, coming out of a watchman's mouth, no doubt gave them a certain sound, and everybody knew the meaning of it, though we do not know it now. It is likely that it was intended to raise attention: he that has an ear to hear, let him hear, as when a lion roars. Or <hi type="italic">he cried as a lion,</hi> very loud and in good earnest, the occasion being very urgent. And what has he to say? 1. He professes his constancy to the post assigned him: "<hi type="italic">I stand, my lord, continually upon the watch-tower,</hi> and have never discovered any thing material till just now; all seemed safe and quiet." Some make it to be a complaint of the people of God that they had long expected the downfall of Babylon, according to the prophecy, and it had not yet come; but withal a resolution to continue waiting; as <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower,</hi> to see what will be the issue of the present providences. 2. He gives notice of the discoveries he had made (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Here comes a chariot of men with a couple of horsemen,</hi> a vision representing the enemy's entry into the city with all their force or the tidings brought to the royal palace of it. <div eID="gen15912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15913" type="x-p"/> V. A certain account is at length given of the overthrow of Babylon. He in the chariot <hi type="italic">answered and said</hi> (when he heard the watchman speak), <hi type="italic">Babylon has fallen, has fallen;</hi> or God answered thus to the prophet enquiring concerning the issue of these affairs: "It has now come to this, Babylon has surely and irrecoverably fallen. Babylon's business is done now. <hi type="italic">All the graven images of her gods he has broken unto the ground.</hi>" Babylon was the mother of harlots (that is, of idolatry), which was one of the grounds of God's quarrel with her; but her idols should now be so far from protecting her that some of them should be broken down to the ground, and others of them, that were worth carrying way, should go into captivity, and be a burden to the beasts that carried them, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2">ch. xlvi. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen15913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15914" type="x-p"/> VI. Notice is given to the people of God, who were then captives in Babylon, that this prophecy of the downfall of Babylon was particularly intended for their comfort and encouragement, and they might depend upon it that it should be accomplished in due season, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">v. 10</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15915" type="x-p"/> 1. The title the prophet gives them in God's name: <hi type="italic">O my threshing, and the corn of my floor!</hi> The prophet calls them <hi type="italic">his,</hi> because they were his countrymen, and such as he had a particular interest in and concern for; but he speaks it as from God, and directs his speech to those that were Israelites indeed, the faithful in the land. Note, (1.) The church is God's floor, in which the most valuable fruits and products of this earth are, as it were, gathered together and laid up. (2.) True believers are the corn of God's floor. Hypocrites are but as the chaff and straw, which take up a great deal of room, but are of small value, with which the wheat is now mixed, but from which it shall be shortly and for ever separated. (3.) The corn of God's floor must expect to be threshed by afflictions and persecutions. God's Israel of old was afflicted from her youth, often under the plougher's plough (<reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Ps. cxxix. 3</reference>) and the thresher's flail. (4.) Even then God owns it for his threshing; it is his still; nay, the threshing of it is by his appointment, and under his restraint and direction. The threshers could have no power against it <hi type="italic">but what was given them from above.</hi> <div eID="gen15915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15916" type="x-p"/> 2. The assurance he gives them of the truth of what he had delivered to them, which therefore they might build their hopes upon: <hi type="italic">That which I have heard of the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel</hi>—that, and nothing else, that, and no fiction or fancy of my own—<hi type="italic">have I declared unto you.</hi> Note, In all events concerning the church, past, present, and to come, we must have an eye to God both as the Lord of hosts and as the God of Israel, who has power enough to do any thing for his church and grace enough to do every thing that is for her good, and to the words of his prophets, as words received from the Lord. As they dare not smother any thing which he has entrusted them to declare, so they dare not declare any thing as from him which he has not made known to them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1 Cor. xi. 23</reference>.
entries.bf9b3878e10bdd1b2706d562ce2c3e046c998ae0: <div eID="gen15916" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Watchman Interrogated. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 714.)</title> <div sID="gen15917" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? <hi type="super">12</hi> The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come. <div eID="gen15917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15918" type="x-p"/> This prophecy concerning Dumah is very short, and withal dark and hard to be understood. Some think that Dumah is a part of Arabia, and that the inhabitants descended from Dumah the sixth son of Ishmael, as those of Kedar (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.16-Isa.21.17">v. 16, 17</reference>) from Ishmael's second son, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.13-Gen.25.14">Gen. xxv. 13, 14</reference>. Others, because Mount Seir is here mentioned, by Dumah understand Idumea, the country of the Edomites. Some of Israel's neighbours are certainly meant, and their distress is foretold, not only for warning to them to prepare them for it, but for warning to Israel not to depend upon them, or any of the nations about them, for relief in a time of danger, but upon God only. We must see all creature confidences failing us, and feel them breaking under us, that we may not lay more weight upon them than they will bear. But though the explication of this prophecy be difficult, because we have no history in which we find the accomplishment of it, yet the application will be easy. We have here, <div eID="gen15918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15919" type="x-p"/> 1. A question put by an Edomite to the watchman. Some one or other <hi type="italic">called out of Seir,</hi> somebody that was more concerned for the public safety and welfare than the rest, who were generally careless and secure. As the man of Macedonia, in a vision, desired Paul to come over and help them (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">Acts xvi. 9</reference>), so this man of Mount Seir, in a vision, desired the prophet to inform and instruct them. He calls not many; it is well there are any, that all are not alike unconcerned about the things that belong to the public peace. Some out of Seir ask advice of God's prophets, and are willing to be taught, when many of God's Israel heed nothing. The question is serious: <hi type="italic">What of the night?</hi> It is put to a proper person, the <hi type="italic">watchman,</hi> whose office it is to answer such enquiries. He repeats the question, as one in care, as one in earnest, and desirous to have an answer. Note, (1.) God's prophets and ministers are appointed to be watchmen, and we are to look upon them as such. They are as watchmen in the city in a time of peace, to see that all be safe, to knock at every door by personal enquiries ("Is it locked? Is the fire safe?"), to direct those that are at a loss, and check those that are disorderly, <reference osisRef="Song.3.3">Cant. iii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.5.7">v. 7</reference>. They are as watchmen in the camp in time of war, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.7">Ezek. xxxiii. 7</reference>. They are to take notice of the motions of the enemy and to give notice of them, to make discoveries and then give warning; and in this they must deny themselves. (2.) It is our duty to enquire of the watchmen, especially to ask again and again, <hi type="italic">What of the night?</hi> for watchmen wake when other sleep. [1.] What time of the night? After a long sleep in sin and security, is it not time to rise, high time to awake out of sleep? <reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Rom. xiii. 11</reference>. We have a great deal of work to do, a long journey to go; is it not time to be stirring? "Watchman, what o'clock is it? After a long dark night is there any hope of the day dawning?" [2.] What tidings of the night? <hi type="italic">What from the night?</hi> (so some); "what vision has the prophet had to-night? We are ready to receive it." Or, rather, "What occurs to night? What weather is it? What news?" We must expect an alarm, and never be secure. The <hi type="italic">day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night;</hi> we must prepare to receive the alarm, and resolve to keep our ground, and then take the first hint of danger, and to our arms presently, to our spiritual weapons. <div eID="gen15919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15920" type="x-p"/> 2. The watchman's answer to this question. The watchman was neither asleep nor dumb; though it was a man of Mount Seir that called to him, he was ready to give him an answer: <hi type="italic">The morning comes.</hi> He answers, (1.) By way of prediction: "There comes first a morning of light, and peace, and opportunity; you will enjoy one day of comfort more; but afterwards comes a night of trouble and calamity." Note, In the course of God's providence it is usual that morning and night are counterchanged and succeed each other. Is it night? Yet the morning comes, and the day-spring knows his place, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Ps. xxx. 5</reference>. Is it day? Yet the night comes also. If there be a morning of youth and health, there will come a night of sickness and old age; if a morning of prosperity in the family, in the public, yet we must look for changes. But God usually gives a morning of opportunity before he sends a night of calamity, that his own people may be prepared for the storm and others left inexcusable. (2.) By way of excitement: <hi type="italic">If you will enquire, enquire.</hi> Note, It is our wisdom to improve the present morning in preparation for the night that is coming after it. "<hi type="italic">Enquire, return, come.</hi> Be inquisitive, be penitent, be willing and obedient." The manner of expression is very observable, for we are put to our choice what we will do: "<hi type="italic">If you will enquire, enquire;</hi> if not, it is at your peril; you cannot say but you have a fair offer made you." We are also urged to be at a point: "If you will, say so, and do not stand pausing; what you will do do quickly, for it is no time to trifle." Those that return and come to God will find they have a great deal of work to do and but a little time to do it in, and therefore they have need to be busy.
entries.095f0b2df971654b92a48b12859d915da161af92: <div eID="gen15920" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Arabia. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 714.)</title> <div sID="gen15921" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim. <hi type="super">14</hi> The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled. <hi type="super">15</hi> For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war. <hi type="super">16</hi> For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Within a year, according to the years of a hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: <hi type="super">17</hi> And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen15921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15922" type="x-p"/> Arabia was a large country, that lay eastward and southward of the land of Canaan. Much of it was possessed by the posterity of Abraham. The <hi type="italic">Dedanim,</hi> here mentioned (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.13">v. 13</reference>), descended from Dedan, Abraham's son by Keturah; the inhabitants of Tema and Kedar descended from Ishmael, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Gen. xxv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.15">15</reference>. The Arabians generally lived in tents, and kept cattle, were a hardy people, inured to labour; probably the Jews depended upon them as a sort of a wall between them and the more warlike eastern nations; and therefore, to alarm them, they shall hear <hi type="italic">the burden of Arabia,</hi> and see it sinking under its own burden. <div eID="gen15922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15923" type="x-p"/> I. A destroying army shall be brought upon them, with a sword, with <hi type="italic">a drawn sword,</hi> with <hi type="italic">a bow</hi> ready <hi type="italic">bent,</hi> and with all the <hi type="italic">grievousness of war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.15">v. 15</reference>. It is probable that the king of Assyria, in some of the marches of his formidable and victorious army, took Arabia in his way, and, meeting with little resistance, made an easy prey of them. The consideration of the grievousness of war should make us thankful for the blessings of peace. <div eID="gen15923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15924" type="x-p"/> II. The poor country people will hereby be forced to flee for shelter wherever they can find a place; so that <hi type="italic">the travelling companies of Dedanium,</hi> which used to keep the high roads with their caravans, shall be obliged to quit them and <hi type="italic">lodge in the forest in Arabia</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.13">v. 13</reference>), and shall not have the wonted convenience of their own tents, poor and weather-beaten as they are. <div eID="gen15924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15925" type="x-p"/> III. They shall stand in need of refreshment, being ready to perish for want of it, in their flight from the invading army: "<hi type="italic">O you inhabitants of the land of Tema!</hi>" (who probably were next neighbours to the companies of Dedanim) "<hi type="italic">bring you water</hi>" (so the margin reads it) "<hi type="italic">to him that is thirsty,</hi> and <hi type="italic">prevent with your bread those that flee,</hi> for they are objects of your compassion; they do not wander for wandering sake, nor are they reduced to straits by any extravagance of their own, but <hi type="italic">they flee from the sword.</hi>" Tema was a country where water was sometimes a scarce commodity (as we find, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job vi. 19</reference>), and we may conclude it would be in a particular manner acceptable to these poor distressed refugees. Let us learn hence. 1. To look for distress ourselves. We know not what straits we may be brought into before we die. Those that live in cities may be forced to lodge in forests; and those may know the want of necessary food who now eat bread to the full. Our mountain stands not so strong but that it may be moved, rises not so high but that it may be scaled. These Arabians would the better bear these calamities because in their way of living they had used themselves to hardships. 2. To look with compassion upon those that are in distress, and with all cheerfulness to relieve them, not knowing how soon their case may be ours: "<hi type="italic">Bring water to those that are thirsty,</hi> and not only give bread to those that need and ask it, but prevent those with it that have need; give it to them unasked." Those that do so shall find it remembered to their praise, as (according to our reading) it is here remembered to the praise of the land of Tema that they did bring water to the thirsty and relieved even those that were on the falling side. <div eID="gen15925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15926" type="x-p"/> IV. All that which is the glory of Kedar shall vanish away and fail. Did they glory in their numerous herds and flocks? They shall all be driven away by the enemy. It seems they were famous about other nations for the use of the bow in battle; but their archers, instead of foiling the enemy, shall fall themselves; and <hi type="italic">the residue of their number,</hi> when they are reduced to a small number, <hi type="italic">shall be diminished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">v. 17</reference>); their mighty able-bodied men, and men of spirit too, shall become very few; for they, being most forward in the defence of their country, were most exposed, and fell first, either by the enemies' sword or into the enemies' hand. Note, Neither the skill of archers (though they be ever so good marksmen) nor the courage of mighty men can protect a people from the judgments of God, when they come with commission; they rather expose the undertakers. That is poor glory which will thus quickly come to nothing. <div eID="gen15926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15927" type="x-p"/> V. All this shall be done in a little time: "<hi type="italic">Within one year according to the years of a hireling</hi> (within one year precisely reckoned) this judgment shall come upon Kedar." If this fixing of the time be of no great use to us now (because we find not either when the prophecy was delivered or when it was accomplished), yet it might be of great use to the Arabians then, to awaken them to repentance, that, like the men of Nineveh, they might prevent the judgment when they were thus told it was just at the door. Or, when it begins to be fulfilled, the business shall be done, be begun and ended in one year's time. God, when he please, can do a great work in a little time. <div eID="gen15927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15928" type="x-p"/> VI. It is all ratified by the truth of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.16">v. 16</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Thus hath the Lord said to me;</hi> you may take my word for it that it is his word;" and we may be sure no word of his shall fall to the ground. And again (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord God of Israel hath spoken it,</hi> as the God of Israel, in pursuance of his gracious designs concerning them; and we may be sure <hi type="italic">the strength of Israel will not lie.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.21"/> <div eID="gen15928" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f561efe00094f2644bf5da7858b88f26df88372: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8676"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.21.1-Isa.21.10">Is 21:1-10</reference>. Repetition of the Assurance Given in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Chapters to the Jews About to Be Captives in Babylon, that Their Enemy Should Be Destroyed and They Be Delivered.</title> <div sID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> He does not narrate the event, but graphically supposes himself a watchman in Babylon, beholding the events as they pass.<div eID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8676"/><hi type="bold">1. desert--</hi>the champaign between Babylon and Persia; it was once a desert, and it was to become so again.<div eID="gen14313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the sea--</hi>The plain was covered with the water of the Euphrates like a "sea" (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.13">Jr 51:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">36</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Is 11:15</reference>, the Nile), until Semiramis raised great dams against it. Cyrus removed these dykes, and so converted the whole country again into a vast desert marsh.<div eID="gen14314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whirlwinds in the south--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.37.9">Job 37:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.14">Zec 9:14</reference>). The south wind comes upon Babylon from the deserts of Arabia, and its violence is the greater from its course being unbroken along the plain (<reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen14315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desert--</hi>the plain between Babylon and Persia.<div eID="gen14316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrible land--</hi>Media; to guard against which was the object of Nitocris' great works [Herodotus, 1.185]. Compare as to "terrible" applied to a wilderness, as being full of unknown dangers, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.29">De 1:29</reference>. <div eID="gen14317" type="x-p"/>
entries.553e438d8b16eff0098a696bc11a0937839da362: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8677"/><div sID="gen14318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8677"/><hi type="bold">2. dealeth treacherously--</hi>referring to the military stratagem employed by Cyrus in taking Babylon. It may be translated, "is repaid with treachery"; then the subject of the verb is Babylon. She is repaid in her own coin; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>, favor this.<div eID="gen14318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go up--</hi>Isaiah abruptly recites the order which he hears God giving to the Persians, the instruments of His vengeance (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen14319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elam--</hi>a province of Persia, the original place of their settlement (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Ge 10:22</reference>), east of the Euphrates. The name "Persia" was not in use until the captivity; it means a "horseman"; Cyrus first trained the Persians in horsemanship. It is a mark of authenticity that the name is not found before Daniel and Ezekiel [Bochart].<div eID="gen14320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereof--</hi>the "sighing" caused by Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.7">Is 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen14321" type="x-p"/>
entries.69f11d520c0cf9889e2ec6a8e9fa391e2fce4279: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8678"/><div sID="gen14322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8678"/>3. Isaiah imagines himself among the exiles in Babylon and cannot help feeling moved by the calamities which come on it. So for Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Is 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">16:11</reference>).<div eID="gen14322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pain--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Is 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.4">Eze 30:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">Na 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the hearing--</hi>The Hebrew may mean, "I was so bowed down that I could not hear; I was so dismayed that I could not see" (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.2">Ge 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14324" type="x-p"/>
entries.b27121ae166ac89c422ac1934b5c528d21476345: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8679"/><div sID="gen14325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8679"/><hi type="bold">4. panted--</hi>"is bewildered" [Barnes].<div eID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night of my pleasure--</hi>The prophet supposes himself one of the banqueters at Belshazzar's feast, on the night that Babylon was about to be taken by surprise; hence his expression, "my pleasure" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jr 51:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>). <div eID="gen14326" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa606700f570a10114598a0fe8cf2d081fa067d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8680"/><div sID="gen14327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8680"/><hi type="bold">5. Prepare the table--</hi>namely, the feast in Babylon; during which Cyrus opened the dykes made by Semiramis to confine the Euphrates to one channel and suffered them to overflow the country, so that he could enter Babylon by the channel of the river. Isaiah first represents the king ordering the feast to be got ready. The suddenness of the irruption of the foe is graphically expressed by the rapid turn in the language to an alarm addressed to the Babylonian princes, "Arise," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Is 22:13</reference>). Maurer translates, "They prepare the table," &c. But see <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Is 8:9</reference>.<div eID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch in ... watchtower--</hi>rather, "set the watch." This done, they thought they might feast in entire security. Babylon had many watchtowers on its walls.<div eID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anoint ... shield--</hi>This was done to prevent the leather of the shield becoming hard and liable to crack. "Make ready for defense"; the mention of the "shield" alone implies that it is the Babylonian revellers who are called on to prepare for instant self-defense. Horsley translates, "Grip the oiled shield." <div eID="gen14329" type="x-p"/>
entries.9346ae6fb42cb0a24248e4bb9ed35b1e95303867: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8681"/><div sID="gen14330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8681"/><hi type="bold">6. Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth--</hi>God's direction to Isaiah to set a watchman to "declare" what he sees. But as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Is 21:10</reference>, Isaiah himself is represented as the one who "declared." Horsley makes him the "watchman," and translates, "Come, let him who standeth on the watchtower report what he seeth." <div eID="gen14330" type="x-p"/>
entries.44535d918a36bf210bd0183fbba1e277527e7cf8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8682"/><div sID="gen14331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8682"/><hi type="bold">7. chariot, &c.--</hi>rather, "a body of riders," namely, some riding in pairs on horses (literally, "pairs of horsemen," that is, two abreast), others on asses, others on camels (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>). "Chariot" is not appropriate to be joined, as English Version translates, with "asses"; the Hebrew means plainly in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>, "a body of men riding." The Persians used asses and camels for war [Maurer]. Horsley translates, "One drawn in a car, with a pair of riders, drawn by an ass, drawn by a camel"; Cyrus is the man; the car drawn by a camel and ass yoked together and driven by two postilions, one on each, is the joint army of Medes and Persians under their respective leaders. He thinks the more ancient military cars were driven by men riding on the beasts that drew them; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference> favors this. <div eID="gen14331" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7a462a99fac8bfa2cfd5a30875eac451047cc98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8683"/><div sID="gen14332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8683"/><hi type="bold">8. A lion--</hi>rather, "(The watchman) cried, I am as a lion"; so as is understood (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Is 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>). The point of comparison to "a lion" is in <reference osisRef="Rev.10.3">Re 10:3</reference>, the loudness of the cry. But here it is rather his vigilance. The lion's eyelids are short, so that, even when asleep, he seems to be on the watch, awake; hence he was painted on doors of temples as the symbol of watchfulness, guarding the place (Hor. Apollo) [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14332" type="x-p"/>
entries.cab4bc97fe34431d7495229e9a6da01f2d2bdc36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8684"/><div sID="gen14333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8684"/><hi type="bold">9. chariot of men--</hi>chariots with men in them; or rather, the same body of riders, horsemen two abreast, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference> [Maurer]. But Horsley, "The man drawn in a car with a pair of riders." The first half of this verse describes what the watchman sees; the second half, what the watchman says, in consequence of what he sees. In the interval between <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>, the overthrow of Babylon by the horsemen, or man in the car, is accomplished. The overthrow needed to be announced to the prophet by the watchman, owing to the great extent of the city. Herodotus (1.131) says that one part of the city was captured some time before the other received the tidings of it.<div eID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answered--</hi>not to something said previously, but in reference to the subject in the mind of the writer, to be collected from the preceding discourse: proclaimeth (<reference osisRef="Job.3.2">Job 3:2</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.26">Da 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.8">Ac 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fallen ... fallen--</hi>The repetition expresses emphasis and certainty (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.9">Psa 92:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3">93:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.8">Jr 51:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images--</hi>Bel, Merodach, &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">Jr 50:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">51:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.52">52</reference>). The Persians had no images, temples, or altars, and charged the makers of such with madness [Herodotus 1.131]; therefore they dashed the Babylonian "images broken unto the ground." <div eID="gen14336" type="x-p"/>
entries.74435715a7f1f4e596b47abec2de63b86da7b433: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8685"/><div sID="gen14337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8685"/><hi type="bold">10. my threshing--</hi>that is, my people (the Jews) trodden down by Babylon.<div eID="gen14337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corn of my floor--</hi>Hebrew, "my son of the floor," that is, my people, treated as corn laid on the floor for threshing; implying, too, that by affliction, a remnant (grain) would be separated from the ungodly (chaff) [Maurer]. Horsley translates, "O thou object of my unremitting prophetic pains." See <reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Is 28:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">28</reference>. Some, from <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jr 51:33</reference>, make Babylon the object of the threshing; but Isaiah is plainly addressing his countrymen, as the next words show, not the Babylonians.<div eID="gen14338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14339" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Is 21:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">12</reference>. A Prophecy to the Idumeans Who Taunted the Afflicted Jews in the Babylonish Captivity.<div eID="gen14339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14340" type="x-p"/> One out of Seir asks, What of the night? Is there a hope of the dawn of deliverance? Isaiah replies, The morning is beginning to dawn (to us); but night is also coming (to you). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>. The Hebrew captives would be delivered, and taunting Edom punished. If the Idumean wish to ask again, he may do so; if he wishes an answer of peace for his country, then let him "return (repent), come" [Barnes]. <div eID="gen14340" type="x-p"/>
entries.70d30a3c22a968e2959e4fe02550b002a67f1128: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8686"/><div sID="gen14341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8686"/><hi type="bold">11. Dumah--</hi>a tribe and region of Ishmael in Arabia (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.14">Ge 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.30">1Ch 1:30</reference>); now called Dumah the Stony, situated on the confines of Arabia and the Syrian desert; a part put for the whole of Edom. Vitringa thinks "Dumah," Hebrew, "silence," is here used for Idumea, to imply that it was soon to be reduced to silence or destruction.<div eID="gen14341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seir--</hi>the principal mountain in Idumea, south of the Dead Sea, in Arabia-Petræa. "He calleth" ought to be rather, "There is a call from Seir."<div eID="gen14342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to me--</hi>Isaiah. So the heathen Balak and Ahaziah received oracles from a Hebrew prophet.<div eID="gen14343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Watchman--</hi>the prophet (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jr 6:17</reference>), so called, because, like a watchman on the lookout from a tower, he announces future events which he sees in prophetic vision (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Ha 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen14344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what of the night--</hi>What tidings have you to give as to the state of the night? Rather, "What remains of the night?" How much of it is past? [Maurer]. "Night" means calamity (<reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.6">Mi 3:6</reference>), which, then, in the wars between Egypt and Assyria, pressed sore on Edom; or on Judah (if, as Barnes thinks, the question is asked in mockery of the suffering Jews in Babylon). The repetition of the question marks, in the former view, the anxiety of the Idumeans. <div eID="gen14345" type="x-p"/>
entries.cff6f441536a14e338244a9a36569f89b9e2b9e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8687"/><div sID="gen14346" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8687"/>12. Reply of the prophet, The morning (prosperity) cometh, and (soon after follows) the night (adversity). Though you, Idumeans, may have a gleam of prosperity, it will soon be followed by adversity again. Otherwise, as Barnes, "Prosperity cometh (to the Jews) to be quickly followed by adversity (to you, Idumeans, who exult in the fall of Jerusalem, have seized on the southern part of their land in their absence during the captivity, and now deride them by your question)" (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.5-Isa.34.7">Is 34:5-7</reference>). This view is favored by Ob 10-21.<div eID="gen14346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ye will inquire, inquire--</hi>If ye choose to consult me again, do so (similar phrases occur in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.14">Ge 43:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.4">2Ki 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.4.16">Es 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen14347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return, come--</hi>"Be converted to God (and then), come" [Gesenius]; you will then receive a more favorable answer.<div eID="gen14348" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.21.13-Isa.21.17">Is 21:13-17</reference>. Prophecy that Arabia Would Be Overrun by a Foreign Foe within a Year.</title> <div sID="gen14349" type="x-p"/> Probably in the wars between Assyria and Egypt; Idumea and Arabia lay somewhat on the intermediate line of march. <div eID="gen14349" type="x-p"/>
entries.381124af6490fb4da09a7fd0e3f81dff9e7cf1e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8688"/><div sID="gen14350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8688"/><hi type="bold">13. upon--</hi>that is, respecting.<div eID="gen14350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest--</hi>not a grove of trees, but a region of thick underwood, rugged and inaccessible; for Arabia has no forest of trees.<div eID="gen14351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">travelling companies--</hi>caravans: ye shall be driven through fear of the foe to unfrequented routes (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Is 33:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.5.6">Jud 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">Jr 49:8</reference> is parallel to this passage).<div eID="gen14352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Dedanim--</hi>In North Arabia (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Ge 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jr 25:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.13">Eze 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">27:20</reference>; a different "Dedan" occurs <reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Ge 10:7</reference>). <div eID="gen14353" type="x-p"/>
entries.4215571ef22520d4a09d911b71b1c4f7df4681e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8689"/><div sID="gen14354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8689"/><hi type="bold">14. Tema--</hi>a kindred tribe: an oasis in that region (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jr 25:23</reference>). The Temeans give water to the faint and thirsting Dedanites; the greatest act of hospitality in the burning lands of the East, where water is so scarce.<div eID="gen14354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prevented--</hi>that is, anticipated the wants of the fugitive Dedanites by supplying bread (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Ge 14:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their bread--</hi>rather, "his (the fugitive's) bread"; the bread due to him, necessary for his support; so "thy grave" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Is 14:19</reference>), [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14356" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f8a329605bacdeb7f5f127ad22519f62bc75e94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8690"/><div sID="gen14357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8690"/><hi type="bold">15. they--</hi>the fugitive Dedanites and other Arabs. <div eID="gen14357" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f54631a74dc80e9e77fcfd37a26d6990bf3f77f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8691"/><div sID="gen14358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8691"/><hi type="bold">16. years of ... hireling--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Is 16:14</reference>).<div eID="gen14358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kedar--</hi>a wandering tribe (<reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Psa 120:5</reference>). North of Arabia-Petræa, and south of Arabia-Deserta; put for Arabia in general. <div eID="gen14359" type="x-p"/>
