he means Chaldea, not that it was deserted or thinly inhabited, but because the Jews had a desert on that side of them; just as if, instead of Italy, we should name “the Alps,” because they are nearer to us, and because we must cross them on our road to Italy. This reason ought to be kept in view; for he does not describe the nature of the country, but forewarns the Jews that the destruction of the enemies, which he foretells, is near at hand, and is as certain as if the event had been before their eyes, as that desert was. Besides, the prophets sometimes spoke ambiguously about Babylon, that believers alone might understand the hidden mysteries, as Jeremiah changes the king’s name.
{Bogus footnote}
As storms from the south. He says from the south, because that wind is tempestuous, and produces storms and whirlwinds.
{Bogus footnote}
When he adds that “it cometh from the desert,” this tends to heighten the picture; for if any storm arise in a habitable and populous region, it excites less terror than those which spring up in deserts. In order to express the shocking nature of this calamity, he compares it to storms, which begin in the desert, and afterwards take a more impetuous course, and rush with greater violence.
Yet the Prophet appears to mean something else, namely, that as they burst forth like storms from that direction to lay Judea desolate, so another storm would soon afterwards arise to destroy them; and therefore he says that this burden will come from a terrible land. By this designation I understand Judea to be meant, for it was not enough to speak of the ruin of Babylon, if the Jews did not likewise understand that it came from God. Why he calls it “a terrible land” we have seen in our exposition of the eighteenth chapter.
{Bogus footnote}
It was because, in consequence of so many displays of the wrath of God, its disfigured appearance might strike terror on all. The occasion on which the words are spoken does not allow us to suppose that it is called “terrible” on account of the astonishing power of God by which it was protected. Although therefore Babylon was taken and plundered by the Persians and Medes, Isaiah declares that its destruction will come from Judea; because in this manner God will revenge the injuries done to that nation of which he had promised to be the guardian.
entries.688fe330fb99be34216afe7a74af9a886e554143: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.2" sID="gen43680" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">A harsh vision.</hi> As the object was to soothe the grief of the people, it may be thought not to be appropriate to call a vision, which is the occasion of joy, <hi type="italic">a harsh vision</hi>. But this refers to the Babylonians, who, puffed up with their prosperity, dreaded no danger; for wealth commonly produces pride and indifference. As if he had said, “It is useless to hold out the riches and power of the Babylonians, and when a stone is hard, there will be found a hard hammer to break it.”<div eID="gen43681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43682" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The spoiler.</hi> As Babylon had gained its power by plundering and laying waste other nations, it seemed to be free from all danger. Although they had been a terror to others, and had practiced every kind of barbarity and cruelty, yet they could not avoid becoming a prey and enduring injuries similar to those which they had inflicted on others. The Prophet goes farther, and, in order to obtain credit to his statements, pronounces it to be a righteous retaliation, that violence should correspond to violence.<div eID="gen43682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43683" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Go up, O Elam.</hi> <hi type="italic">Elam</hi> is a part of Persia; but is taken for the whole of Persia, and on this account also the Persians are called Elamites. It is worthy of observation, that, when Isaiah foretold these things, there was no probability of war, and that he was dead a hundred years before there was any apprehension of this calamity. Hence it is sufficiently evident that he could not have derived his information on this subject from any other than the Spirit of God; and this contributes greatly to confirm the truth and certainty of the prediction.<div eID="gen43683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43684" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Besiege, O Mede.</hi> By commanding the Medes and Persians, he declares that this will not befall the Babylonians at random or by chance, but by the sure decree of God, in whose name, and not in that of any private individual, he makes the announcement. Coming forward therefore in the name of God, he may, like a captain or general, command his soldiers to assemble to give battle. In what manner God employs the agency of robbers and wicked men, has been formerly explained at the tenth chapter. <note n="66"> <div sID="gen43685" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43685" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen43684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43686" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">I have made all his groaning to cease.</hi> Some understand it to mean, that the groaning, to which the Babylonians had given occasion, ceased after they were subdued by the Medes and Persians; for by their tyrannical measures they had caused many to groan, which must happen when wicked and ungodly men possess rank and power. Others approach more closely, perhaps, to the real meaning of the Prophet, when they say, that “the groaning ceased,” because the Babylonians experienced no compassion, having formerly shewn none to others. But I explain it more simply to mean, that the Lord was deaf to their groanings; as if he had said, that there would be no room for their groanings and lamentations, because having been cruel and barbarous, it was just that they should receive back the same measure which they had meted out to others. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.2">Matthew 7:2</reference>.)<div eID="gen43686" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43680" osisID="Isa.21.2" type="section"/>
entries.79eb87a8cdaebd6b0df75e3da5687078432e5420: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.3" sID="gen43687" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore are my loins, filled with pain.</hi> Here the Prophet represents the people as actually present, for it was not enough to have simply foretold the destruction of Babylon, if he had not confirmed the belief of the godly in such a manner that they felt as if the actual event were placed before their eyes. Such a representation was necessary, and the Prophet does not here describe the feelings of his own heart, as if he had compassion on the Babylonians, but, on the contrary, as we have formerly said, <note n="67"> <div sID="gen43689" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43689" type="x-p"/> </note> he assumes, for the time, the character of a Babylonian. <note n="68"> <div sID="gen43690" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43690" type="x-p"/> </note> It ought undoubtedly to satisfy our minds that the hidden judgments of God are held out to us, as in a mirror, that they may arouse the sluggishness of our faith; and therefore the Prophets describe with greater beauty and copiousness, and paint in lively colors, those things which exceed the capacity of our reason. The Prophet, thus expressing his grief, informs believers how awful is the vengeance of God which awaits the Chaldeans, and how dreadfully they will be punished, as we are struck with surprise and horror when any sad intelligence is brought to us.<div eID="gen43688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43691" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As the pangs of a woman that travaileth.</hi> He adds a stronger expression of grief, when he compares it to that of a woman in labor, as when a person under fearful anguish turns every way, and writhes in every part of his body. Such modes of expression are employed by the Prophets on account of our sluggishness, for we do not perceive the judgments of God till they be pointed at, as it were, with the finger, and affect our senses. We are warned to be on our guard before they arrive.<div eID="gen43691" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43687" osisID="Isa.21.3" type="section"/>
entries.f055d6158bf004398b932189cb1d70b929a50315: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.4" sID="gen43692" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">My heart was shaken.</hi> Others render it not amiss, “my heart wandered;” for excessive terror moves the heart, as it were, out of its place. He declares how sudden and unlooked for will be the destruction of Babylon, for a sudden calamity makes us tremble more than one which has been long foreseen and expected. Daniel relates, that what Isaiah here foretells was accomplished, and that he was an eye-witness. Belshazzar had that night prepared a magnificent banquet, when the Persians suddenly rushed upon him, and nothing was farther from his expectation than that he would be slain. High delight was thus suddenly changed into terror. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.5.30">Daniel 5:30</reference>.)<div eID="gen43693" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43692" osisID="Isa.21.4" type="section"/>
entries.e418f72b08ccbf1730f949848acfd6bf197698c2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.5" sID="gen43694" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">Prepare the table.</hi> These verbs may be taken for participles; as if he had said, “While they were preparing the table and appointing a guard, while they were eating and drinking, sudden terror arose; there was a call to arms, Arise ye princes,” etc.. But Isaiah presents lively descriptions, so as to place the actual event, as it were, before our eyes. Certainly Xenophon does not describe so historically the storming of the city; and this makes it evident that it was not natural sagacity, but heavenly inspiration, that taught Isaiah to describe so vividly events that were unknown. Besides, we ought to observe the time when these predictions were uttered; for at that time the kingdom of Babylon was in its most flourishing condition, and appeared to have invincible power, and dreaded no danger. Isaiah ridicules this vain confidence, and shews that this power will speedily be laid in ruins.<div eID="gen43695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43696" type="x-p"/>Let it not be thought absurd that he introduces the watchmen as speaking; for although the siege had not shaken off the slothfulness of a proud and foolish tyrant so as to hinder him from indulging in gaiety and feasting, still there is no room to doubt that men were appointed to keep watch. It is customary indeed with princes to defend themselves by guards, that they may more freely and without any disturbance abandon themselves to every kind of pleasure; but the Prophet expressly mixes up the sentinels with the delicacies of the table, to make it more evident that the wicked tyrant was seized with a spirit of giddiness before he sunk down to drunken reveling. The king of Babylon was thus feasting and indulging in mirth with his courtiers, when he was overtaken by a sudden and unexpected calamity, not that he was out of danger, but because he disregarded and scorned the enemy. The day before it happened, it might have been thought incredible, for the conspiracy of Gobryas, and of that party which betrayed him, had not yet been discovered. At the time when Isaiah spoke, none would have thought that an event so extraordinary would ever take place.<div eID="gen43696" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43694" osisID="Isa.21.5" type="section"/>
entries.58921d50582a62d0c3eccdb64c5ac0172f59a5da: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.6" sID="gen43697" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">For thus hath the Lord said to me.</hi> The Prophet is commanded to set a <hi type="italic">watchman</hi> on the watchtower, to see these things at a distance; for they cannot be perceived by the eyes, or learned by conjecture. In order, therefore, that all may know that he did not speak at random, he declares that he foretells these things; for although they are unknown to men, and incredible, yet he clearly and distinctly knows them by the spirit of prophecy, because he is elevated above the judgment of men. This ought to be carefully observed; for we must not imagine that the prophets learned from men, or foresaw by their own sagacity, those things which they made known; and on this account also they were justly called “Seers.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.9">1 Samuel 9:9</reference>.) Though we also see them, yet our sight is dull, and we scarcely perceive what is at our feet; and even the most acute men are often in darkness, because they understand nothing but what they can gather by the use of reason. But the prophets speak by the Spirit of God, as from heaven. The amount of what is stated is, that whosoever shall attempt to measure this prophecy by their own judgment will do wrong, because it has proceeded from God, and therefore it goes far beyond our sense.<div eID="gen43698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43699" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Go, appoint a watchman.</hi> It gives additional weight that he “appoints a watchman in the name of God.” If it be objected, “You relate incredible things as if they had actually happened,” he replies that he does not declare them at random; for he whom the prince has appointed to be a watchman, sees from a distance what others do not know. Thus Isaiah saw by the revelation of the Spirit what was unknown to others.<div eID="gen43699" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43697" osisID="Isa.21.6" type="section"/>
entries.e2360dbdaccefaf55baa91ee1c18ad23726ae432: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.7" sID="gen43700" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he saw a chariot.</hi> What he now adds contains a lively description of that defeat. Some think that it is told by the king’s messenger. This is a mistake; for the Prophet, on the contrary, foretells what he has learned from the watchman whom he appointed by the command of God. Here he represents the watchman as looking and reporting what he saw. As if at the first glance he had not seen it clearly, he says that there is “a chariot,” and afterwards observing more closely, he says that there is “a couple of horses” in the chariot. At first, on account of the novelty and great distance of the objects, the report given is ambiguous and confused; but afterwards, when a nearer view is obtained, they are better understood. There is no absurdity in applying to prophets or to divine visions what belongs to men; for we know that God, accommodating himself to our feeble capacity, takes upon himself human feelings.<div eID="gen43701" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43700" osisID="Isa.21.7" type="section"/>
entries.c78a2bb6599dbb2f1ded762456b9c687249866ac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.8" sID="gen43702" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he cried, A lion. </hi>“Having hearkened diligently with much heed,” at length he observes <hi type="italic">a</hi> <hi type="italic">lion</hi>. This is supposed to mean Darius who conquered and pillaged Babylon, as we learn from Daniel. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.5.28 Bible:Dan.5.31">Daniel 5:28, 31</reference>.)<div eID="gen43703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43704" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">I stand continually.</hi> When the watchman says that he is continually on his watchtower by day and by night, this tends to confirm the prediction, as if he had said that nothing can be more certain than this vision; for they whom God has appointed to keep watch are neither drowsy nor dim-sighted. Meanwhile, by this example, he exhorts and stimulates believers to the same kind of attention, that by the help of the lamp of the word, they may obtain a distant view of the power of God.<div eID="gen43704" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43702" osisID="Isa.21.8" type="section"/>
entries.5117b6f77d41642c2d062ec7b31b860bd36326a0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.9" sID="gen43705" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi><hi type="italic"> Babylon is fallen, is fallen.</hi> This shews plainly that it is not king Belshazzar’s watchman who is introduced, for this speech would be unsuitable to such a character. The Prophet therefore makes known, by the command of God, what would happen. Now, this may refer either to God or to Darius, as well as to the watchman; and it makes little difference as to the meaning, for Darius, being God’s servant in this matter, is not inappropriately represented to be the herald of that judgment. There would be greater probability in referring it to God himself; for Darius had no such thoughts when he overthrew the idols of the Babylonians. But the speech agrees better with the character of a guardian, as if an angel added an interpretation to the prophecy.<div eID="gen43706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43707" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And all the graven images of her gods.</hi> There is here an implied contrast between the living God and dead idols. This mode of expression, too, deserves notice, when he calls them “images of gods;” for the Babylonians knew, as all idolaters loudly proclaim, that their images are not gods. Yet they ascribed to them divine power, and when this is done, “the truth of God is changed into a lie,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.25">Romans 1:25</reference>,) and not only so, but God himself is denied. But on this subject we shall afterwards speak more largely. Here we see, that by her destruction Babylon was punished for idolatry, for he assigns the reason why Babylon was destroyed. It was because the Lord could not endure that she should glory in her “graven images.”<div eID="gen43707" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43705" osisID="Isa.21.9" type="section"/>
entries.b2e418864f5afc608843e4dadfedc66029edb391: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.10" sID="gen43708" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">My thrashing, and the son of my floor.</hi> <note n="69"> <div sID="gen43710" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43710" type="x-p"/> </note> The wealth of that powerful monarchy having dazzled the eyes of all men by its splendor, what Isaiah foretold about its destruction might be reckoned fabulous. He therefore leads their minds to God, in order to inform them that it was God who had undertaken to destroy Babylon, and that it is not by the will of men, but by divine power, that such loftiness will fall to the ground. The “thrashing” and “the son of the floor” mean the same thing; for this mode of expression is frequently employed by Hebrew writers, who often repeat the same statement in different language.<div eID="gen43709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43711" type="x-p"/>This passage ought to be carefully observed, that we may correct a vice which is natural to us, that of measuring the power of God by our own standard. Not only does our feebleness place us far below the wisdom of God; but we are wicked and depraved judges of his works, and cannot be induced to take any other view of them than of what comes within the reach of the ability and wisdom of men. But we ought always to remember his almighty power, and especially when our own reason and judgment fail us. Thus, when the Church is oppressed by tyrants to such a degree that there appears to be no hope of deliverance, let us know that the Lord will lay them low, and, by trampling on their pride and abasing their strength, will shew that they are his “thrashing-floor;” for the subject of this prediction was not a person of mean rank, but the most powerful and flourishing of all monarchies. The more they have exalted themselves, the more quickly will they be destroyed, and the Lord will execute his “thrashing” upon them. Let us learn that what the Lord has here given as a manifestation of inconceivable ruin, applies to persons of the same stamp.<div eID="gen43711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43712" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That which I have heard from the Lord of hosts.</hi> When he says that he has “heard it from the Lord of hosts,” he sets a seal, as it were, on his prophecy; for he declares that he has not brought forward his own conjectures, but has received it from the Lord himself. Here it is worthy of our notice, that the servants of God ought to be fortified by this boldness to speak in the name of God, as Peter also exhorts, “He that speaketh, let him speak as the oracles of God.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.4.11">1 Peter 4:11</reference>.) Impostors also boast of the name of God, but his faithful servants have the testimony of their conscience that they bring forward nothing but what God has enjoined. Observe, also, that this confirmation was highly necessary, for the whole world trembled at the resources of this powerful monarchy.<div eID="gen43712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43713" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">From the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel.</hi> It is not without reason that he gives to God these two appellations. As to the former, it is indeed a title which always applies to God; but here, undoubtedly, the Prophet had his eye on the matter in hand, in order to contrast the power of God with all the troops of the Babylonians; for God has not a single army, but innumerable armies, to subdue his enemies. Again, he calls him “the God of Israel,” because by destroying Babylon he shewed himself to be the defender and guardian of his people; for the overthrow of that monarchy procured freedom for the Jews. In short, all these things were done for the sake of the Church, which the Prophet has here in view; for it is not the Babylonians, who undoubtedly laughed at these predictions, but believers, whom he exhorts to rest assured that, though they were oppressed by the Babylonians, and scattered and tossed about, still God would take care of them.<div eID="gen43713" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43708" osisID="Isa.21.10" type="section"/>
entries.81850ad6c65aba965b7698e6320b3220522a14e0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.11" sID="gen43714" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">The burden of Dumah. </hi>It is evident from <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.14">Genesis 25:14</reference>, that this nation was descended from a son of Ishmael, to whom this name was given, and hence his posterity are called Dumeans. <note n="70"> <div sID="gen43716" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43716" type="x-p"/> </note> The cause of their destruction, which is here foretold, cannot be known with certainty, and this prophecy is obscure on account of its brevity. Yet we ought always to remember what I have formerly remarked, that it was proper that the Jews should be fortified against the dreadful stumbling-blocks which were approaching. When so many changes take place, particularly if the world is turned upside down, and if there is a rapid succession of events, we are perplexed and entertain doubts whether all things happen at random and by chance, or are regulated by the providence of God. The Lord therefore shews that it is he who effects this revolution, and renews the state of the world, that we may learn that nothing here is of long duration, and may have our whole heart and our whole aim directed to the reign of Christ, which alone is everlasting.<div eID="gen43715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43717" type="x-p"/>Since therefore these changes were near at hand, it was proper that the Jews should be forewarned, that when the event followed, they should call them to remembrance, contemplate the wisdom of God, and strengthen their faith. Besides, there is no room to doubt that the Jews were harassed by various thoughts, when they saw the whole world shaken on all sides, and desired to have some means of avoiding those storms and tempests; for we always wish to be in safety and beyond the reach of danger. Some might have wished to find new abodes, that they might better provide for their own safety; but when storms raged on every hand, they were reminded to remain at home, and to believe that no safer habitation could anywhere be found than in the company of the godly.<div eID="gen43717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43718" type="x-p"/>This example ought also to be a warning to many who separate themselves from the Church through fear of danger, and do not consider that a greater danger awaits them out of it. These thoughts might therefore distress the Jews, for we have seen in the eighth chapter that their minds were restless. <note n="71"> <div sID="gen43719" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43719" type="x-p"/> </note> When they were thus tossed about in uncertainty, and fleeing to foreign nations, they would naturally lose heart; and this, I think, is the chief reason why the destruction of the Dumeans is foretold, namely, that the Jews might seek God with their whole heart, and that above all things they might commit to his care the safety of the Church. Let us therefore learn to keep ourselves within the Church, though she be afflicted by various calamities, and let us bear patiently the fatherly chastisements which are inflicted on children, instead of choosing to go astray, that we may drink the dregs which choke the wicked. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.75.8">Psalm 75:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.51.17">Isaiah 51:17</reference>.) What shall become of strangers and reprobates, if children are thus chastised? (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.4.17 Bible:1Pet.4.18">1 Peter 4:17, 18</reference>.) Yet it is possible that the chosen people suffered some molestation from the people of God, when their neighbors assailed them on every side.<div eID="gen43718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43720" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Out of Seir.</hi> Mount Seir, as we learn from the book of Genesis, was a mountain of the Edomites. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.6 Bible:Gen.32.3 Bible:Gen.36.8 Bible:Gen.36.9">Genesis 14:6; 32:3; 36:8, 9</reference>.) Under the name of this mountain he includes the whole kingdom. In this place he represents, as in a picture, those things which called for an earnest address.<div eID="gen43720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43721" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Watchman, what of the night?</hi> It is probable that the Edomites, who put the question, were not at a great distance from them, and that they were solicitous about the danger as one in which they were themselves involved. He introduces them as inquiring at the “watchman,” not through curiosity, but with a view to their own advantage, what he had observed in “the night,” just as when one has asked a question, a second and a third person follow him, asking the same thing. This is the meaning of the repetition, that the inquiry is made not by one individual only, but by many persons, as commonly happens in cases of doubt and perplexity, when every man is afraid on his own account, and does not believe what is said by others.<div eID="gen43721" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43714" osisID="Isa.21.11" type="section"/>
entries.dd9c7c8b3c91e6efe7171f98bd2f9aaf3136bc73: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.12" sID="gen43722" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">The morning cometh.</hi> This means that the anxiety will not last merely for a single day, or for a short time, as if the watchman had replied, “What I tell you to-day, I will tell you again to-morrow; if you are afraid now, you will also be afraid to-morrow.” It is a most wretched condition when men are tortured with anxiety, in such a manner that they hang in a state of doubt between death and life; and it is that dismal curse which the Lord threatens against wicked men by Moses,<div eID="gen43723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43724" type="x-p"/>“Would that I lived till the evening; and in the evening, would that I saw the dawn!” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.67">Deuteronomy 28:67</reference>.)<div eID="gen43724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43725" type="x-p"/>The godly indeed are beset with many dangers, but they know that they and their life are committed to the hand of God, and even in the jaws of death they see life, or at least soothe their uneasy fears by hope and patience. But the wicked always tremble, and not only are tormented by alarm, but waste away in their sorrows.<div eID="gen43725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43726" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Return, come.</hi> These words may be explained in two ways; either that if they run continually, they will lose their pains, or in this way, “If any among you be more careful, let them go to Dumah, and there let them tremble more than in their native country, for nowhere will they be safe.” But since God always takes care of his Church, nowhere shall we find a safer retreat, even though we shall compass sea and land.<div eID="gen43726" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43722" osisID="Isa.21.12" type="section"/>
entries.ba4773fce8f61ca48a9f640be8a0023f57a504f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.13" sID="gen43727" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13. </hi><hi type="italic">The burden upon Arabia.</hi> He now passes on to the Arabians, and foretells that they too, in their own turn, will be dragged to the judgment-seat of God; so that he does not leave unnoticed any of the nations which were known to the Jews. He declares that they will be seized with such fear that they will leave their houses and flee into the woods; and he states the direction in which they will flee, that is, to “Dedanim.”<div eID="gen43728" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43727" osisID="Isa.21.13" type="section"/>
entries.3fa458171328241ecf856826c38e1ebecbd930af: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.14" sID="gen43729" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> <hi type="italic">To meet the thirsty bring waters.</hi> <note n="72"> <div sID="gen43731" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43731" type="x-p"/> </note> He heightens the description of that trembling with which the Lord had determined to strike the Arabians in such a manner that they thought of nothing but flight, and did not take time even to collect those things which were necessary for the journey. Isaiah therefore declares that the Arabians will come into the country of Dedanim, empty and destitute of all things, and that they will not be provided with any food. On this account he exhorts the inhabitants to go out and meet them with bread and water, because otherwise they will faint through the want of the necessaries of life.<div eID="gen43730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43732" type="x-p"/>I am aware that this passage is explained differently by some commentators, who think that the Prophet mocks at the Arabians, who had been cruel and barbarous towards the Jews; as if he had said, “How gladly you would now bring water to the thirsty!” But that exposition is too constrained. And yet I do not deny that they received the reward of their cruelty, when they ran hither and thither in a state of hunger. But the meaning which I have given is twofold, <note n="73"> <div sID="gen43733" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43733" type="x-p"/> </note> that the Arabians in their flight will be so wretched that they will not even have the necessary supply of water, and they will therefore faint with thirst, if they do not quickly receive assistance; and he intimates that there will be a scarcity both of food and of drink. He calls on the neighbors to render assistance; not to exhort them to do their duty, but to state the fact more clearly; and he enjoins them to give their bread to them, not because it is deserved, but because they are suffering extreme want. Yet as it is founded on the common law of nature and humanity, the Prophet indirectly insinuates that the hungry and thirsty are defrauded of their bread, when food is denied to them.<div eID="gen43732" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43729" osisID="Isa.21.14" type="section"/>
entries.240c57f78df60bf0801fe03fafe5f3a437e8b93e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.15" sID="gen43734" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">For they flee from the face of the swords.</hi> <note n="74"> <div sID="gen43736" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43736" type="x-p"/> </note> He means that the calamity will be dreadful, and that the Arabians will have good reason for betaking themselves to flight, because the enemies will pursue them with arms and with swords, so that they will have no other way of providing for their safety than by flight. The reason why he foretells this defeat is plain enough; for it was necessary that the Jews should obtain early information of that which should happen long after, that they might learn that the world is governed by the providence of God and not by chance, and likewise that they should be taught by the example of others to behold God as the judge of all nations, wherever they turned their eyes. We do not know, and history does not inform us, whether or not the Arabians were enemies of the Jews. However that may be, it is certain that these things are spoken for the consolation of the godly, that they may behold the justice of God towards all nations, and may acknowledge that his judgment-seat is at Jerusalem, from which he will pronounce judgment on the whole world.<div eID="gen43735" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43734" osisID="Isa.21.15" type="section"/>
entries.4f333448911b2a44077f2f7116e5180df1e041f5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.21.16" sID="gen43737" type="section"/> <div sID="gen43738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16. </hi><hi type="italic">For thus hath the Lord said to me.</hi> He adds that this defeat of the Arabians, of which he prophesied, is close at hand; which tended greatly to comfort the godly. We are naturally fiery, and do not willingly allow the object of our desire to be delayed; and the Lord takes into account our weakness in this respect, when he says that he hastens his work. He therefore declares that he prophesies of things which shall happen, not after many ages, but immediately, that the Jews may bear more patiently their afflictions, from which they know that they will be delivered in a short time.<div eID="gen43738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43739" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Yet a year according to the years of the hireling.</hi> Of the metaphor of “the year of the hireling,” which he adds for the purpose of stating the matter more fully, we have already spoken. <note n="75"> <div sID="gen43740" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43740" type="x-p"/> </note> It means that the time will not be delayed. The same comparison is used by heathen authors, where they intend to describe a day appointed and desired; as appears from that passage in Horace, “The day appears long to those who must render an account of their work.” <note n="76"> <div sID="gen43741" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen43741" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen43739" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.21.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen43737" osisID="Isa.21.16" type="section"/>
entries.d56e3d27a809ee98f737a70f5797faf1c7389ace:
17. And the residue of the archers. He threatens that this slaughter will not be the end of their evils, because if there be any residue in Arabia, they will gradually decrease; as if he had said, “The Lord will not merely impoverish the Arabians by a single battle, but will pursue to the very utmost, till all hope of relief is taken away, and they are utterly exterminated.” Such is the vengeance which he executes against the ungodly, while he moderates the punishment which he inflicts on the godly, that they may not be entirely destroyed.
Of the mighty men. He means warlike men and those who were fit to carry arms, and says, that although they escaped that slaughter, still they will be cut off at their own time. He formerly threatened similar chastisements against the Jews, but always accompanied by a promise which was fitted to alleviate their grief or at least to guard them against despair. It frequently happens that the children of God are afflicted as severely as the reprobate, or even with greater severity; but the hope of favor which is held out distinguishes them from the whole world. Again, when we learn that God visits on the wicked deadly vengeance, this is no reason why we should be immoderately grieved even at the heaviest punishments; but, on the contrary, we ought to draw from it this consolation, that he chastises them gently, and “does not give them over to death.” (Psalm 118:18.)
The God of Israel hath spoken it. The Prophet shews, as we have frequently remarked on former occasions, that we ought not only to acknowledge that these things happened by divine appointment, but that they were appointed by that God whom Israel adores. All men are sometimes constrained to rise to the acknowledgment of God, though they are disposed to believe in chance, because the thought that there is a God in heaven comes into their minds, whether they will or not, and that both in prosperity and in adversity; but then they imagine a Deity according to their own fancy, either in heaven or on earth. Since therefore irreligious men idly and foolishly imagine a God according to their own pleasure, the Prophet directs the Jews to that God whom they adore, that they may know the distinguished privilege which they enjoy in being placed under his guardianship and protection. Nor is it enough that we adore some God as governor of the world, but we must acknowledge the true God, who revealed himself to the fathers, and hath manifested himself to us in Christ. And this ought to be earnestly maintained, in opposition to the profane thoughts of many persons who contrive some strange and confused notion of a Deity, because they dare not openly deny God.
CHAPTER 22
Isaiah Chapter 22:1-25
1. The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the house-tops?
1. Onus vallis visionis. Quid tibi hic, (vel, nunc?) quia tu universa conscendisti super tecta?
2. Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.
2. Strepituum plena, urbs turbulenta, civitas exultans; interfecti tui non interfecti gladio, et non mortui in prælio.
3. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far.
3. Cuncti principes tui profugerunt parita ab arcu; vincti sunt. Omnes, inquam, in te reperti vincti sunt pariter, qui a longinquo fugerunt.
4. Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people.
4. Propterea dixi, Desistite a me; amarus ero in fletu meo, ne contendatis me consolari super vastatione filiæ populi mei.
5. For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains.
5. Quoniam dies perturbationis, et conculcationis, et anxietatis Domino Iehovæ exercituum in valle visionis, diruenti urbem, et clamor ad montem.
6. And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield.
6. Atqui Elam portans pharetram in curru hominis, equitum, inquam, et Ceir nudans clypeum.
7. And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate.
7. Et fuit ut electio vallium tuarum repleta sit curribus, et equites instruendo instruerent ad portam.
8. And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest.
8. Et transtulit operimentum Iuda; et respexisti in die illa ad armaturam domus saltus.
9. Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many; and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool:
9. Et interruptiones civitatis David vidistis, quæ multæ erant; et collegistis aquas piscinæ inferioris.
10. And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall.
10. Et domos Ierusalem numerastis; et domos diruistis ad muniendum murum.
11. Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago.
11. Fossam quoque fecistis inter muros, aquis piscinæ veteris, et non respexistis ad fictorum ejus, et opificem ejus ab antiquo (vel, eminus) non vidistis.
12. And in that day did the Lord God of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth:
12. Porro vocavit Dominus Iehova exercituum in die isto ad fletum et lamentum, ad calvitium et cincturam sacci.
13. And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen and killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we shall die.
13. Et ecce gaudium et lætitia, occidere bovem, mactare ovem, edere carnes, et bibere vinum, comedere, inquam, et bibere; quia cras moriemur.
14. And it was revealed in mine ears by the Lord of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord God of hosts.
14. Id revelatum est auribus Iehovæ exercituum, Si remittetur vobis hæc iniquitas, donec moriamini, dicit Dominus Iehova exercituum.
15. Thus saith the Lord God of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say,
15. Sic dicit Dominus Iehova exercituum, Vade, ingredere ad fautorem istum, ad Sabna præfectum domus.
16. What hast thou here, and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
16. Quid tibi hic? et quis tibi hic? quod tibi hic excideris sepulchrum, sicut qui in excelso excidit sepulchrum suum, aut qui in rupe sculpit habitaculum sibi.
17. Behold, the Lord will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee.
17. Ecce Iehova traducet te traductione insigni, et operiendo operiet te.
18. He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house.
18. Convolvendo volvet te convolutione, quasi globam in terram longinquam manibus; ibi morieris; et ibi currus gloriæ tuæ ignominia domus domini tui.
19. And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.
19. Et propulsabo te de statione tua, et de sede tua te expellet.
20. And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah;
20. Et erit in die illa: vocabo servum meum Eliakim, filium Helciæ.
21. And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand; and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah.
21. Et induam eum vestibus tuis, et balteo tuo roborabo eum; et potestatem tuam tradam in manum ejus, et erit pater incolæ Ierusalem et domi Iuda.
22. And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder: so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
22. Et ponem clavem domus David super humerum ejus; aperiet, et nemo claudet; claudet, et nemo aperiet.
23. And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house.
23. Et figam eum veluti clavum in loco fideli; eritque in solium gloriæ domui patris sui.
24. And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons.
24. Et suspendent ab eo omnem gloriam domus patris sui, nepotes et pronepotes, omnia vasa minora, a vasis craterarum ad cuncta vasa melodiarum.
25. In that day, saith the Lord of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the Lord hath spoken it
25. In die illa, dicit Iehova exercituum, recedet clavus fixus in loco fideli, frangetur et cadet, et dissipabitur onus quod fuit super ipsum; quia Iehova loquutus est.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="21" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:582" />
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>THE burden of the desert of the sea <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> as is evident both from her destroyers, the <ns0:hi>Medians, v.</ns0:hi> 2. and especially from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. where she is na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med. She seems to be called <ns0:hi>Desert</ns0:hi> Prophetically, to inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate, that although she was now a most Popular City and Kingdom, yet shortly she should be turned into a Desolate Wilderness, as was threatned <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 13. 19. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But the Word here rendred <ns0:hi>Desert</ns0:hi> sometime signifies <ns0:hi>a Plain,</ns0:hi> as a very learned Interpreter hath observed, and thus it most properly agrees to <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> and the Land about it, which Geographers note to be a very plain Country, without any Considerable Mountains in it. It is called <ns0:hi>the Desert of the Sea,</ns0:hi> because it is scituate by the Sea, as <ns0:hi>the Isles of the Sea, Est.</ns0:hi> 10. 1. are those Countries which were beside the Sea. And the Title of <ns0:hi>the Sea</ns0:hi> might well be given to the Wa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> because of the great plenty and multitude of them, the great Channel of <ns0:hi>Euphrates,</ns0:hi> and the several lesser Channels cut out, and the vast Lakes of Water; in which respects it is said to <ns0:hi>sit upon many waters, Ier.</ns0:hi> 51. 13. the Name of <ns0:hi>sea</ns0:hi> being given by the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> to every great Collection of Waters.</ns0:note>. As <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 9 14.</ns0:note> whirlewinds in the south <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In those Parts which lay South<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward from <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> where there were many and great De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sarts, in which the Winds have greater force. See <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 19. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 4. 11.</ns0:note> pass through <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As meeting with no stop or opposition.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> it <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Burden or Judgment. Or, <ns0:hi>he,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Median,</ns0:hi> as it is in the next Verse.</ns0:note> cometh from the desert <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">From <ns0:hi>Media</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persia;</ns0:hi> thus expressed, either because those Countries were full of Desarts, or be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause a great Desart lay between them and <ns0:hi>Chaldaea,</ns0:hi> as Geo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />graphers and Historians report.</ns0:note>, from a terrible land <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">From the <ns0:hi>Medes,</ns0:hi> a war<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />like and formidable People, as appears both from Sacred and Prophane Writers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 A <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> hard.</ns0:note> grievous vision <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A Vision or Prophecy, containing dreadful Calamities which were to fall upon <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> is declared unto me, the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This is spoken either, 1. of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> as their Sin, for which God sends the following Judgment: So the sence is, The <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> still persist in the Practice of Treachery and Rapine, to which they have been so long accustomed: Or, 2. of the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians,</ns0:hi> who are here noted to pay the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> in their own Coin, and to use the same Treachery and Vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence towards them, which they had done to others. To which purpose the Words are and may well be rendred otherwise, either thus, <ns0:hi>The treacherous dealer</ns0:hi> hath found <ns0:hi>a treacherous dealer, and the spoiler</ns0:hi> hath found <ns0:hi>a spoiler:</ns0:hi> or thus, <ns0:hi>O thou that dealest treacherously with the treacherous dealer, and that spoilest the spoiler, go up, O Elam, &c.</ns0:hi> as it followeth. These Words will be much illustrated by comparing them with <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 33. 1. There is no doubt to be made, but the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> used Treachery as well as Force against <ns0:hi>Babylon:</ns0:hi> And besides other Instances now unknown, we have one upon Record, of their entertaining those two Traytors, <ns0:hi>Gadatas</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gobrias,</ns0:hi> and following their Counsel and Conduct in taking the City, which made them Parta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kers of their Treason.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 17.</ns0:note> Go up <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To fight against her. These are God's Words, either giving them Command and Commissi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to do so, or rather foretelling what they would do; which is oft done in this form of Speech.</ns0:note>, O Elam <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Persia,</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Elam</ns0:hi> Synechdochically, because <ns0:hi>Elam</ns0:hi> was an eminent Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vince of <ns0:hi>Persia,</ns0:hi> bordering upon the <ns0:hi>Medes.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>; Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siege <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon, v.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note>, O Media; all the sighing thereof <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either, 1. <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> sighing, which shall cease, because they shall have no time to sigh, or lament their Miseries, being suddenly surprised, and cut off in a mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, as they were. As God is said to <ns0:hi>seek out the wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> of wicked men <ns0:hi>till he find none, Psal.</ns0:hi> 10. 15. when he utterly destroyeth them in or with their Sins: Or, 2. the sighing and groanings of God's People, and other Nations under the heavy Oppressions of that potent and cruel Em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pire; the Pronoun <ns0:hi>her,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>thereof,</ns0:hi> being taken here not pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sively, as commonly it is; but actively, or efficiently, as sometimes it is, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 11. 25. <ns0:hi>your fear, i. e.</ns0:hi> the fear of you; and <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 33. 7. <ns0:hi>my terrour, i. e.</ns0:hi> the terrour or dread of me upon thee.</ns0:note> have I made to cease.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Therefore are my Ioins <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which he mentions with respect to the following Simi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />litude of childbearing, in which the loins are sorely pain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed. And this the Prophet speaks, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ither 1. in the Name and Person of the <ns0:hi>Babylonian.</ns0:hi> Or rather, 2. in his own Name; which is most natural, and agrees best with the last clause of the Verse, which plainly speaks of the tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment which he had in the meer hearing of the Word, and seeing the Vision, and not of that which they had in the feeling of it; although the latter is implied in the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer; and the Prophet expresseth his horrour in hearing and seeing, to intimate the dreadful horrour which should seize upon them when it came upon them.</ns0:note> filled with pain; pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travelleth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Sharp and grievous pains.</ns0:note> I was <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> wri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thed.</ns0:note> bowed down at the hearing <ns0:hi>of it,</ns0:hi> I was dismayed at the seeing <ns0:hi>of it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ind wandred.</ns0:note> My heart panted, fearfulness afrighted me: the night of my pleasure <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The night, in which I used to have a sweet Repose and Sleep. He seems to have had this Vision in a night. But withal this horrour of the Prophet by night was Typical, and did signifie that grievous horrour and destruction, which should befal the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> in a night of great Feasting and Jollity, as it did <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 5. 1, 30.</ns0:note> hath he <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">God, who shewed him that Vision.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> put.</ns0:note> turned into fear <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Into a time and matter of fear.</ns0:note> unto me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Prepare the table <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Furnish it with Meats and Drinks, as it follows. The Prophet foretells what the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> would be doing when their Enimies were at their Doors, that they would give up themselves to Feasting and Security.</ns0:note>, watch in the watch-tow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To give us notice of any approaching danger, that in the mean time we may more securely indulge our selves in Mirth and Pleasures.</ns0:note>, eat, drink: arise, ye Princes <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, 1. ye <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians:</ns0:hi> Whilst your Enemies the <ns0:hi>Babylonian</ns0:hi>'s are feasting securely, prepare to make your Assault. Or, 2. ye Princes of <ns0:hi>Babylon:</ns0:hi> Arise from the Table and run to your Arms. Which sudden a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larm and change of their Posture proceeded from Tidings out of the Watch-tower, as may be gathered from the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer Clause, and is more fully expressed in the following Verses.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> anoint the shield <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Prepare your selves and your Arms for the Battel approaching. <ns0:hi>The shield</ns0:hi> is put for all their weapons of Offence and Defence. They used to Anoint their Shields with Oyl, partly to preserve and polish them; and partly to make them slippery, that their Enemies Darts might not fasten in them, but slide off from them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 For thus hath the Lord said unto me <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I speak not my own fancies, but what God hath made me to see and hear in a Vision; the Particulars whereof are related in the following Verses.</ns0:note>, Go, set a watchman <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either, 1. a Prophet; such being oft so called, as <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 3. 17. & 33. 2. Or rather, 2. a Military Watchman. For this was now done onely in a Vision, which yet did foresignifie what should be done really afterwards.</ns0:note>, let him declare <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To thee in Vision, to them Really.</ns0:note> what he seeth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And he saw <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A short Speech, for, He told me that he saw.</ns0:note> a chariot <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not for Burden, but for War, in which Chariots were then much used.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> a couple of horse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Attended with two Horse-men. So there were both Chariots and Troops of Horsemen. Or, with <ns0:hi>a couple of horses,</ns0:hi> as this Word is sometimes used, as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam..</ns0:hi> 8. 11. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 6. The Chariot was drawn with two Horses.</ns0:note>, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Two Chariots, one drawn by Asses, (under which Title some understand Mules, as being engendred of Asses) and the other by Camels. Whereby he signifies the Variety and Abundance of Warlike Provisions which the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> should have for this Expedition, and particularly of Chariots, whereof some were for the Carriage of Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary Things, and others for the Battel.</ns0:note>; and he hearkned diligently <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He carefully observed what he saw, and what he could further discover.</ns0:note> with much heed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And he <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> cried as a lion.</ns0:note> cried, A lion <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The sence of the Words thus rendred is this, The Watchman cried out, I see also a Lion, to wit, marching be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the Horsemen and Chariots already mentioned: which they suppose to represent <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Darius</ns0:hi> marching in the Head of their Armies.</ns0:note>: my lord <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, as it is rendred in the Mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gin, and by divers others, <ns0:hi>he cried</ns0:hi> as (which Particle is oft understood, as hath been formerly and frequently noted) <ns0:hi>a lion,</ns0:hi> with a terrible Cry, as being affrighted with the Vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion, and withal signifying the dreadfulness of that Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment which was here represented as coming upon <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Watchman speaks these Words either to God, or to the Prophet, who by command from God had set him in this Place and Station; to whom therefore he gives the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing Account of his Discharge of the Work wherewith he was intrusted.</ns0:note>, I stand continually upon the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hab. 2. 1.</ns0:note> watch-tower in the day-time, and I am set in my ward <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> every night.</ns0:note> whole nights <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">According to thy Command I have stood, and do yet stand continually, both day and night, up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on my Watch-Tower.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:583" />9 And behold <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The sum of what I have discovered is this.</ns0:note>, here cometh a chariot of men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not fil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led with Goods, as Chariots of Burden use to be; but pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viden with Men, to fight from or with them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> a couple of horsemen <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand, <ns0:hi>and a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels;</ns0:hi> which is easily understood from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. where they are expressed.</ns0:note>: and he <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Prophet <ns0:hi>Isaias,</ns0:hi> who set the Watchman; or the Lord, by whose Command he was set, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. who here gives an Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plication of the Vision.</ns0:note> answered and said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 51. 8. Rev. 14. 8. & 18. 2.</ns0:note> Babylon is fallen, is fallen: and all the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 46. 1. Jer. 50. 2. & 51. 44.</ns0:note> graven images of her gods <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which is mentioned as an Evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence that she was fully conquered, because otherwise they would not have suffered their Idols to have been thrown to the Ground.</ns0:note> he <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">God, by the Hands of <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> his Instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment. Or, it is an indefinite Speech, <ns0:hi>he hath broken, &c.</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>they are broken, &c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> hath broken unto the ground.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 O my threshing <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Threshing</ns0:hi> is here put for the Corn threshed, as it is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plained in the following Words, the Act being frequently put for the Object, as <ns0:hi>captivity</ns0:hi> for the Captives, <ns0:hi>fear</ns0:hi> for the thing seared, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> as hath been noted before. And the Corn threshed is here metaphorically put for People sorely affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cted and punished, which is oft expressed by Threshing, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 25. 10. & 41. 15. <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 4. 13. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> This is spoken ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> to whom he now turneth his Speech, whom God did grievously thresh and afflict by the <ns0:hi>Babylo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nians,</ns0:hi> and whom he here comforts with these Tidings, as if he had said, Though thou wilt be threshed first, yet <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> shall be threshed last, and most dreadfully, and their Thresh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing shall be thy Deliverance. This Interpretation is thought necessary, because of the latter Clause of the Verse, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with this is to be joined. Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 2. of <ns0:hi>Babylon. O my threshing:</ns0:hi> or, thou art <ns0:hi>my threshing,</ns0:hi> whom I have undertaken to thresh and punish. And so this is fitly mentioned here, to assure them that this Prophecy of <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> Fall must necessarily be accomplished, because the Almighty was engaged in the Work. And this Interpretation seems not to be incon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sistent with the rest of the Verse, as we shall see.</ns0:note>, and the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> son.</ns0:note> corn of my floor <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Corn which I will cause to be threshed upon the Floor. Heb. <ns0:hi>the son of my floor.</ns0:hi> For the Title of <ns0:hi>son</ns0:hi> is oft given to lifeless things, as Arrows are called <ns0:hi>the sons of the bow,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>of the quiver, Iob</ns0:hi> 5. 7. &. 41. 28. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">What I have foretold is not my own Invention, but the Word of God, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore shall infallibly come to pass.</ns0:note> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to you <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either, 1. unto you my People, or Hearers; for all the Prophecies, even con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning other Nations, were published to them, and for their Use and Comfort: Or, 2. Unto (or, Concerning, as this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Particle is sometimes used, as the Learned know) you <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> to whom this was in some sort de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clared, because it was published amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and by their means might easily come to the knowledge of other People, and consequently of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> Nor is it un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />usual for the Prophets, in their Prophecies delivered to God's People concerning <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> by an <ns0:hi>Apostrophe</ns0:hi> to turn their Speech to the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> themselves; of which we have Instances, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 24, 31. & 51. 13, 14, 25, 26.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 The burden of Dumah <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, 1. of a part of <ns0:hi>Arabia,</ns0:hi> so called from <ns0:hi>Dumah,</ns0:hi> one of <ns0:hi>Ismael</ns0:hi>'s Race, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25. 14. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 1. 30. Or rather, 2. of <ns0:hi>Edom</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Idumea,</ns0:hi> as seems most probable from the men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of Mount <ns0:hi>Seir,</ns0:hi> which was a part of <ns0:hi>Edom;</ns0:hi> which may be here called <ns0:hi>Dumah,</ns0:hi> either by an abbreviation, or cutting off the first Letter from <ns0:hi>Idumea,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Ram</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>Aram,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 2. 9. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 32. 2. or rather prophetically and sarca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stically; for <ns0:hi>Dumah</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>silent:</ns0:hi> Whereby he intimates, That <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> which was much given to vain boasting and railing against God, and against his People, as we read else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where, should be brought to silence and utter ruine. And such new, and enigmatical<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and significant Names are else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where given by the Prophets to divers known Places, as <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>Sheshach, Ier.</ns0:hi> 25. 26. and <ns0:hi>Egypt, Mazer, Mich.</ns0:hi> 7. 12. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>. He <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>Dumah,</ns0:hi> or the People of <ns0:hi>Du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mah,</ns0:hi> of whom he speaks, or one of them in the name and by the appointment of the rest.</ns0:note> calleth to me <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To the Watchman, as appears by the following Words: For the Prophet delivers his Prophecy in the form of a Dialogue between the People and the Watchman.</ns0:note> out of Seir <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Out of <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> which is frequently called <ns0:hi>Seir,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 32. 3. & 36. 8. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20. 20, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> & 25. 11.</ns0:note>, Watchman <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Whereby he means either, 1. the Prophet <ns0:hi>Isaiah,</ns0:hi> whom they call <ns0:hi>watchman,</ns0:hi> either seriously, or in scorn, because the Prophets were so called by God, and by the People of the Jews: Or, 2. the Watchman of <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> whom they had set as People use to do in Times of great Danger.</ns0:note>, what of the night <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>The night</ns0:hi> is taken either, 1. metaphorically, for a time of Tri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bulation. So they ask the Prophet what he hath to say concerning that Night of Calamity which he had so long and oft threatned to them, whereof as yet they saw no ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance: Or, 2 properly; <ns0:hi>the night</ns0:hi> being the proper and chief time in which the Watchman's Care is most necessary, because then their Enemies had opportunity to do them most harm. So the People are supposed to come to him very early in the morning, to inquire what hath hapned in the Night; which shews a State of great Perplexity and Fear: which might well be called a <ns0:hi>burden,</ns0:hi> both because Fear in it self is a great Torment, and because this Fear was a Sign and Presage of their approaching Miseries.</ns0:note>? watchman, what of the night <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The repetition of the same Words, shews the greatness of their Solicitude and Fear.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Night is past without any great mischief to you, and the comfortable Light of the Morning is approaching, which freeth mens Minds from the Terrours of the Night; but although the Morning be coming<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it will be gone, and the Night will return, and your Fears with it. The <ns0:hi>night</ns0:hi> seems to be here taken properly, as <ns0:hi>the morning</ns0:hi> is; yet so, that he alludes to the Metaphorical Signification of the Word, and intimates, that the Night of Affliction was co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ming upon them.</ns0:note>: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">If this Watchman be the Prophet <ns0:hi>Isalas,</ns0:hi> then the sence of these Words is this, <ns0:hi>If you will be enquiring, enquire</ns0:hi> sincerely and seriously of God, by me, concerning your Danger, and the way to prevent it; <ns0:hi>re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turn</ns0:hi> unto the Lord by true Repentance, who alone can se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure you, and <ns0:hi>come</ns0:hi> unto me for Direction. But if it be their own Watchman, which, with submission, I conceive most probable, the sence is, <ns0:hi>If you will enquire, enquire;</ns0:hi> I perceive, by what I have observed this Night, that your Danger is not past, and there will be occasion for further Enquiries from time to time; and therefore <ns0:hi>return, come, i. e.</ns0:hi> either <ns0:hi>return</ns0:hi> to them that sent you with this Message, and then <ns0:hi>come</ns0:hi> to me for further Tydings; or, come again, as <ns0:hi>return, lie down,</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>lie down again,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 5. come to me the next Morning, as you have reason to do, and so from Morning to Morning; for I see every Night is likely to bring some evil Tidings to you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
